h1: What to bring to a beer festival and what to leave at home
title: What to Bring to a Beer Festival | Craft Beer School
desc: A practical checklist of what to bring to a beer festival and what to leave at home, from ID and water to the car keys you should not need.
teaser: The most important thing to bring to a beer festival is a plan for getting home.
standfirst: A good beer festival is a day of small pours, new breweries and long queues. A few things in your bag make it far better. A few things left at home make it safer.
sections:
Before packing anything, decide how you are getting home. A cab, the metro, a friend who is not drinking or a hotel within walking distance. Book or agree it before the day. Leave the car keys at home if you plan to drink. If you are the driver, enjoy the soft drinks and food and do not taste.

Festivals end with crowds at the exit and surge pricing on cabs. Leaving a little before closing time or waiting inside until the rush clears both work. Share your live location with a friend if you are heading home alone.

• Government photo ID. Organisers check age at the gate. The legal drinking age varies by state in India.
  • A charged phone and a power bank. Tickets, tokens, payments and cabs all live on your phone.
  • Some cash as well as UPI. Networks can fail in a crowd.
  • A refillable water bottle, if the event allows one. Most festivals have water points.
  • Sun protection for daytime outdoor events: a cap, sunglasses and sunscreen.
  • A light rain layer in the monsoon.
  • Comfortable shoes. You will stand and queue for hours.
Bring a way to take notes

Festivals pour dozens of beers. By the fifth taster, they blur. A small notebook or a notes app solves that. Write the brewery, beer name, style and three words: aroma, flavour and finish. Add a score out of five.

Those notes are the most valuable thing you bring home. A week later you will know which breweries to visit and which styles you liked. Our guide to growlers and crowlers helps if a brewery you discover sells beer to take away.

• The car keys, unless you are the sober driver.
  • Outside alcohol. Festivals almost always ban it and it may be confiscated at the gate.
  • Large bags. Many events limit bag size and search bags on entry.
  • Valuables you do not need. Crowds and spilled beer are hard on jewellery and expensive gadgets.
  • Glass containers of any kind.

Check the organiser's own page for its specific list. Rules vary from event to event.
Plan your route through the stalls

Most festivals publish a list of breweries and sometimes beers before the day. Spend ten minutes with it. Mark five or six beers you really want to try and note where those stalls are once you see the site map. Get to them early. Popular and limited beers often run out by mid-afternoon.

Then leave room for discovery. Some of the best beers at any festival come from breweries you have never heard of. A good rule is one planned beer, then one surprise.

Queue smart. Lines are shortest when the gates open and during peak food times. Avoid the rush in the last hour, when everyone tries to use up their tokens at once. If you have tokens left over, share them with a friend rather than racing through them. Leftover tokens are a cheap price for a clear head the next morning.

Festival pours are small, often 100 to 150 ml, which makes them easy to underestimate. Ten tasters of 6% beer add up to a lot of alcohol over an afternoon. Decide on a number before you go and stick to it.

Eat early and keep eating. Drink a glass of water between tasters. Start with lighter beers and work up to the strong ones. Our guide to storing beer at home covers what to do with any cans or bottles you buy on the way out.

Go with friends and agree a meeting point in case phones die or you get separated. Keep an eye on anyone who has had too much and get them water, food and a ride home. Festival staff and first-aid teams are there to help, so use them.

Be kind to the brewers. Most are working long shifts at a stall. A quick question about how they made the beer usually gets a good answer.

The best way to use a festival is to taste with a goal: try every IPA, or every wheat beer, or one beer from every brewery you have never heard of. Comparing beers side by side teaches you more than wandering from stall to stall.

The gap most people hit is describing what they taste. Training your nose on reference aromas makes festival notes sharper and far more useful.

Your first step: before your next festival, decide how you are getting home and pick one style you want to compare across every stall.
faqs: Can I bring my own drinks to a beer festival?
Almost never. Most festivals ban outside alcohol and may confiscate it at the gate. Check the organiser's rules.
How many tasters is too many at a festival?
Decide on a number before you go. Small pours add up quickly, so eat, drink water between tasters and stop well before you feel drunk.
Do I need ID at an Indian beer festival?
Yes. Organisers check age at entry and the legal drinking age varies by state, so carry a government photo ID.
